meta.author: Learn in Curve (original authorship)
meta.syllabus: APM Project Fundamentals Qualification Handbook, APM-QS-PFQ-8 V5, April 2026
meta.provenance: All 60 questions written independently against the published PFQ syllabus. No stem, option or distractor is copied from APM's sample exam paper or from any third-party question set. The sample paper was used only to calibrate style, length and difficulty.
notes: Exactly one question per learning outcome, except 10.4 which has two (Tuckman and Belbin) to fill the 60th slot.
The doubled outcome must NOT be hardcoded as 10.4 in the mock generator — see PFQ_DAY_PLAN.md.
type: 'single' = four options, one correct. type: 'multi_select' = four numbered items, options are combinations (APM's fourth presentation style).
trap flags: 'negative_stem' and 'multi_select' are used by Trap School to build targeted drills.
meta.option_order: Stored order is a deterministic shuffle (seed 20260813). Explanations reference option CONTENT, never letters, because the app re-shuffles options per attempt. Never reintroduce letter references.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines a project?

options.a: A permanent organisational function that delivers repeatable outputs.
options.b: A group of related activities managed together to make better use of shared resources.
options.c: Any piece of work that is funded from a separate organisational budget.
options.d: A unique, transient endeavour undertaken to bring about change and achieve planned objectives.

questions.explanation: A project is unique and transient — a defined beginning and end, existing to deliver change. The permanent-function distractor is business as usual, the shared-resources one is a programme, and the separate-budget one describes a funding arrangement rather than a project.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a difference between a project and business as usual?

options.a: A project has a budget, whereas business as usual does not.
options.b: A project has stakeholders, whereas business as usual does not.
options.c: A project produces outputs, whereas business as usual produces none.
options.d: A project has a defined start and end, whereas business as usual is ongoing.

questions.explanation: Transience is the defining difference. Budgets, stakeholders and outputs exist in both — those distractors are true of business as usual too.

questions.stem: Project management can be defined as the application of:

options.a: tools that ensure a project is delivered within its original budget.
options.b: processes, methods, skills, knowledge and experience to achieve specific project objectives.
options.c: techniques used to keep routine operations running within agreed tolerances.
options.d: governance structures that control how an organisation spends its money.

questions.explanation: The APM definition centres on applying processes, methods, knowledge, skills and experience to achieve objectives. The 'ensure delivery within the original budget' distractor is a common trap — project management does not guarantee an outcome.

questions.stem: The key purpose of project management is to:

options.a: remove uncertainty from change initiatives.
options.b: ensure that all available resources are fully utilised at all times.
options.c: keep existing services running to an agreed standard.
options.d: achieve project objectives within agreed constraints, delivering beneficial change.

questions.explanation: Project management exists to effect beneficial change within constraints. Uncertainty is managed, never removed; keeping existing services running is business as usual; and full resource utilisation is a resource-management aim, not the purpose of project management.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes portfolio management?

options.a: Selecting and prioritising projects and programmes so that they align with strategic objectives.
options.b: Delivering repeatable services to an agreed standard within tolerances.
options.c: Applying processes and methods to deliver one defined set of objectives.
options.d: Coordinating related projects to deliver outcomes that could not be achieved by managing them individually.

questions.explanation: Portfolio management is about selection and prioritisation against strategy. The 'coordinating related projects' distractor is the definition of programme management — the classic near-miss for this outcome. The other two describe project management and business as usual.

questions.stem: A project manager would use a PESTLE analysis in order to:

options.a: define the acceptance criteria for the project's outputs.
options.b: prioritise identified risks by probability and impact.
options.c: identify factors in the external environment that could affect the project.
options.d: assess the capability and skill mix of the project team.

questions.explanation: PESTLE (political, economic, sociological, technological, legal, environmental) is a scan of the external operating environment. It may feed risk identification, but it is not itself a prioritisation technique.

questions.stem: Which of the following shows the phases of a typical linear project life cycle in the correct order?

options.a: Definition, deployment, transition, concept.
options.b: Concept, deployment, definition, transition.
options.c: Concept, definition, deployment, transition.
options.d: Definition, concept, deployment, transition.

questions.explanation: Concept, definition, deployment, transition. The sequencing questions are pure recall — learn the order as a phrase, not by reasoning it out under time pressure.

questions.stem: Which phase appears in a typical iterative project life cycle but not in a typical linear one?

options.a: Transition.
options.b: Development.
options.c: Concept.
options.d: Definition.

questions.explanation: An iterative life cycle replaces a single definition-then-deployment run with repeated development iterations. Concept, definition and transition all appear in the linear life cycle too.

questions.stem: A hybrid life cycle can be defined as one that:

options.a: repeats a single phase until the sponsor authorises closure.
options.b: adds adoption and benefits realisation to a linear life cycle.
options.c: removes the concept phase in order to shorten delivery.
options.d: combines elements of linear and iterative life cycles.

questions.explanation: Hybrid = linear plus iterative in one life cycle. The 'adoption and benefits realisation' distractor defines an extended life cycle — hybrid and extended are the most commonly confused pair in LO2.

questions.stem: An extended project life cycle is one that:

options.a: adds adoption and benefits realisation phases to a linear life cycle.
options.b: combines linear and iterative approaches within a single project.
options.c: adds a feasibility study before the concept phase.
options.d: lengthens the deployment phase to allow for late changes in scope.

questions.explanation: 'Extended' means extended past handover, into adoption and benefits realisation — the project is not finished when the output is delivered. The 'combines linear and iterative' distractor is a hybrid life cycle.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a responsibility of the project management office (PMO)?

options.a: Prioritising the requirements to be delivered in the next iteration.
options.b: Providing standards, processes, tools and support across projects.
options.c: Owning the business case and being accountable for realising the benefits.
options.d: Authorising changes that fall outside the project manager's delegated authority.

questions.explanation: The PMO is a supporting and standard-setting function. Owning the business case is the sponsor, prioritising requirements is the product owner, and authorising changes beyond delegated authority is the governance board. Every option here is a role named in outcome 3.1 — this single mark requires knowing all seven.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the term 'deployment baseline'?

options.a: The record of every change request raised during the project.
options.b: The first estimate of cost produced during the concept phase.
options.c: The approved plan against which project progress is measured and controlled.
options.d: The point at which project outputs are handed over to the users.

questions.explanation: A baseline is the reference point for control. Note how plausible the handover distractor sounds — the word 'deployment' invites you to think about go-live. Read the whole option before choosing.

questions.stem: How does the deployment baseline typically differ between a linear and an iterative life cycle?

options.a: In an iterative life cycle it is agreed only at handover.
options.b: In an iterative life cycle it is fixed at the outset and cannot be changed.
options.c: A linear life cycle does not use a deployment baseline at all.
options.d: In a linear life cycle it is set once for the whole project; in an iterative life cycle it is set for each iteration.

questions.explanation: Linear baselines the whole scope up front; iterative baselines each iteration in turn. The 'fixed at the outset and cannot be changed' distractor inverts the two.

questions.stem: Why is the project sponsor a stakeholder of the project management plan?

options.a: Because the sponsor approves the plan and owns the business case that it delivers.
options.b: Because the sponsor supplies the goods and services the plan depends on.
options.c: Because the sponsor writes the plan on the project manager's behalf.
options.d: Because the sponsor carries out the day-to-day activities described in the plan.

questions.explanation: The project manager produces the plan; the sponsor approves it and owns the business case behind it. The 'supplies goods and services' distractor describes suppliers, who are also stakeholders of the plan but for a different reason.

questions.stem: Which of the following would typically be found in a project business case?

options.a: The detailed work breakdown structure for every work package.
options.b: The signed acceptance certificates for completed deliverables.
options.c: The justification for the project, including its costs, benefits and risks.
options.d: The daily log of issues raised by members of the project team.

questions.explanation: The business case answers 'why should we do this, and is it still worth doing'. Costs, benefits, risks, options and timescales — not delivery detail.

questions.stem: In relation to the business case, the project manager is responsible for:

options.a: approving the business case at each decision gate.
options.b: providing the information the sponsor needs in order to develop and maintain it.
options.c: realising the benefits set out in it after handover.
options.d: owning the business case for the duration of the project.

questions.explanation: The sponsor owns, develops and maintains the business case; the project manager supplies the information that keeps it accurate. Owning, approving and realising benefits are all sponsor responsibilities.

questions.stem: Stakeholder analysis supports effective stakeholder engagement because it:

options.a: identifies stakeholders' interest and influence so that engagement can be targeted.
options.b: transfers responsibility for communication to the project sponsor.
options.c: guarantees that every stakeholder will support the project.
options.d: removes the need for a separate communication plan.

questions.explanation: Analysis tells you who matters, how much, and in what way — so effort goes where it changes the outcome. Beware absolute words like 'guarantees' and 'removes the need for'; they are almost always wrong.

questions.stem: Benefits management can be defined as the identification, definition, planning, tracking and realisation of:

options.a: resource costs.
options.b: project risks.
options.c: business benefits.
options.d: project outputs.

questions.explanation: Short-stem definition recall. Outputs are what the project delivers; benefits are the measurable improvement that results from using them.

questions.stem: Which of the following are typical estimating methods?

options.a: 2, 3 and 4
options.b: 1, 2 and 3
options.c: 1, 3 and 4
options.d: 1, 2 and 4

questions.explanation: Analytical (bottom-up), analogous (comparative) and parametric are the three named in the syllabus. 'Incremental' is a delivery approach, not an estimating method. In multi-select questions, find the one item you are certain is wrong and eliminate every option containing it.

questions.stem: The purpose of the estimating funnel is to show that:

options.a: contingency should be removed once the plan has been baselined.
options.b: estimates become more accurate as the project progresses and more becomes known.
options.c: estimates only need to be produced once, at the start of the project.
options.d: project costs always reduce as the project progresses.

questions.explanation: The funnel narrows: early estimates carry wide ranges, later ones narrow as uncertainty falls. It is a statement about accuracy, not about cost reduction.

questions.stem: Establishing success criteria at the start of a project is important because they:

options.a: determine which supplier should be selected.
options.b: fix the project budget for the whole of the life cycle.
options.c: remove the need to produce a business case.
options.d: provide the measures against which the project will ultimately be judged.

questions.explanation: Success criteria define what 'done well' means before anyone has an incentive to redefine it. They are revisited during delivery and at handover — that is why this outcome names all three points.

questions.stem: One benefit of project progress reporting is that it:

options.a: gives stakeholders timely information on performance against the plan.
options.b: prevents any variance from the baseline from occurring.
options.c: removes the need to maintain a risk register.
options.d: ensures the project will be delivered on time.

questions.explanation: Reporting makes performance visible so decisions can be made early. It does not prevent variance — it reveals it.

questions.stem: Scope management can be defined as the process for:

options.a: assessing whether project outputs are fit for purpose.
options.b: recording all costs incurred by the project.
options.c: determining the sequence in which project activities are carried out.
options.d: identifying, defining and controlling the work required to deliver the project's objectives.

questions.explanation: Scope management covers what is in, what is out, and how that boundary is controlled. The sequencing distractor is scheduling; the fitness-for-purpose one is quality control.

questions.stem: Which statement describes how scope is managed in an iterative project rather than a linear one?

options.a: Changes to scope are not permitted once the baseline has been agreed.
options.b: The scope is fixed at the outset and altered only through formal change control.
options.c: The scope of work is defined once, in the product breakdown structure.
options.d: Requirements are re-prioritised within a fixed time and cost.

questions.explanation: Iterative fixes time and resources and flexes scope; linear fixes scope and flexes time and cost through change control. The three distractors all describe linear scope management.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a product breakdown structure (PBS) and a work breakdown structure (WBS)?

options.a: A PBS is used on iterative projects; a WBS is used on linear projects.
options.b: A PBS shows costs; a WBS shows durations.
options.c: A PBS lists project risks; a WBS lists project issues.
options.d: A PBS shows the products to be delivered; a WBS shows the work needed to deliver them.

questions.explanation: Products versus work. Both are hierarchical decompositions used to illustrate scope — the distinction is what sits in the boxes.

questions.stem: A responsibility assignment matrix (RAM) is produced by combining the work breakdown structure with the:

options.a: risk breakdown structure.
options.b: organisational breakdown structure.
options.c: cost breakdown structure.
options.d: product breakdown structure.

questions.explanation: WBS (the work) × OBS (the people) = RAM (who does what). Learning that equation covers most of what this outcome can ask.

questions.stem: Change control can be defined as the process that ensures:

options.a: the current version of every project document is recorded and retrievable.
options.b: all requested changes are identified, evaluated and then approved or rejected before implementation.
options.c: issues are escalated to the sponsor within agreed tolerances.
options.d: the schedule is re-baselined at the end of each phase.

questions.explanation: Change control is a decision process. The 'record the current version of every document' distractor describes configuration management — the pair this outcome most often tests against each other.

questions.stem: What is the relationship between change control and configuration management?

options.a: Configuration management records and tracks the items that change control authorises changes to.
options.b: Configuration management approves the changes that change control identifies.
options.c: Change control replaces configuration management on iterative projects.
options.d: They are two names for the same process.

questions.explanation: Change control decides; configuration management keeps the record straight so everyone knows which version is current. The distractor that has configuration management approving changes reverses the two responsibilities.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stage in a typical change control process?

options.a: Verification audit of the configuration library.
options.b: Realisation of the expected business benefits.
options.c: Evaluation of the request for change.
options.d: Status accounting of controlled items.

questions.explanation: Request, evaluation, recommendation, decision, implementation, update. The verification audit and status accounting distractors are configuration management activities — the examiner deliberately mixes the two lists.

questions.stem: Which of the following are activities in a typical configuration management process?

options.a: 2, 3 and 4
options.b: 1, 2 and 4
options.c: 1, 2 and 3
options.d: 1, 3 and 4

questions.explanation: The five activities are planning, identification, control, status accounting and verification audit. 'Justification' belongs to the business case, not to configuration management.

questions.stem: The purpose of scheduling is to:

options.a: assign ownership of each identified risk.
options.b: define the acceptance criteria for project deliverables.
options.c: determine when activities will take place and what resources they require.
options.d: record the actual cost of each completed work package.

questions.explanation: Scheduling answers when, in what order, and with what. Cost recording, acceptance criteria and risk ownership belong to other processes.

questions.stem: Critical path analysis is used to identify:

options.a: the resources that have been over-allocated across the schedule.
options.b: the risks with the highest combined probability and impact.
options.c: the activities that consume the largest share of the budget.
options.d: the sequence of activities that determines the shortest possible project duration.

questions.explanation: The critical path is the longest path through the network and therefore the shortest time the project can take. Activities on it have zero float — delay one, delay the project.

questions.stem: The primary purpose of a milestone is to:

options.a: record the resources assigned to a work package.
options.b: mark a significant event or the completion of a key deliverable.
options.c: show how much float is available on an activity.
options.d: identify the longest path through the schedule network.

questions.explanation: A milestone has no duration and consumes no resource — it is a marker of significance used for reporting and control.

questions.stem: In a time box, which of the following are fixed?

options.a: Time and scope, with resources and quality allowed to vary.
options.b: Scope and quality, with time and resources allowed to vary.
options.c: Quality and resources, with time and scope allowed to vary.
options.d: Time and resources, with scope and quality allowed to vary.

questions.explanation: A time box fixes the period and the resource, and delivers whatever can be completed to an agreed standard within it. The 'scope and quality fixed' distractor is the linear, change-controlled model — the exact inversion.

questions.stem: Which resource optimisation technique is used when the project completion date must not move, and resource usage is made as even as possible within available float?

options.a: Resource levelling.
options.b: Resource aggregation.
options.c: Resource smoothing.
options.d: Resource estimation.

questions.explanation: Smoothing protects the end date and flexes resource usage within float. Levelling does the opposite — it respects a resource limit and lets the end date move. If the question mentions a fixed date, the answer is smoothing.

questions.stem: A procurement strategy sets out:

options.a: the schedule of payments due to members of the project team.
options.b: the detailed contractual terms agreed with each individual supplier.
options.c: the high-level approach to securing the goods and services the project requires.
options.d: the criteria used to accept delivered products from suppliers.

questions.explanation: Strategy is the high-level approach — make or buy, contract type, supplier relationships. Detailed contractual terms sit beneath the strategy, not in it.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the term 'risk'?

options.a: A measured difference between planned and actual progress.
options.b: An uncertain event that, if it occurs, would affect the achievement of objectives.
options.c: An approved change to the agreed scope of work.
options.d: A problem that is currently affecting delivery and requires resolution.

questions.explanation: Risk is uncertain and forward-looking, and can be a threat or an opportunity. The 'problem currently affecting delivery' distractor is an issue — expect the risk and issue definitions to be used as each other's distractors.

questions.stem: The purpose of risk management is to:

options.a: remove all uncertainty from the delivery of the project.
options.b: record every problem that occurs during delivery.
options.c: minimise threats to, and maximise opportunities for, the project's objectives.
options.d: transfer accountability for project outcomes to the sponsor.

questions.explanation: Both halves matter — risk management is not only about threats. The 'remove all uncertainty' distractor overreaches: uncertainty is managed, never eliminated.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stage in a typical risk management process?

options.a: Risk verification.
options.b: Risk aggregation.
options.c: Risk closure.
options.d: Risk justification.

questions.explanation: The four stages named in the syllabus are identification, analysis, response and closure. The three distractors borrow words from the business case, quality and resource vocabularies.

questions.stem: A risk register is used to:

options.a: hold the record of all approved changes to the project baseline.
options.b: record identified risks, their assessment, their owners and the planned responses.
options.c: capture the lessons learned at the end of the project.
options.d: list the issues that have been escalated to the project sponsor.

questions.explanation: A register is a live control document, not an archive. Each entry carries an owner and a response — a list of risks with no owners is not a risk register.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines the term 'issue'?

options.a: A disagreement between the project team and one of its suppliers.
options.b: A problem that arises only after the project has formally closed.
options.c: An uncertain event that may occur at some point in the future.
options.d: A problem that has occurred and now requires resolution beyond the project manager's delegated tolerances.

questions.explanation: An issue has already happened and typically breaches delegated tolerance, which is why it is escalated. The 'may occur in the future' distractor is a risk.

questions.stem: The purpose of issue management is to:

options.a: prevent any issues from arising during delivery.
options.b: record approved changes to the configuration of deliverables.
options.c: ensure that issues are identified, escalated and resolved so objectives can still be met.
options.d: assess the probability and impact of events that have not yet happened.

questions.explanation: Issue management is about resolution, not prevention — you cannot prevent something that has already occurred. The probability-and-impact distractor describes risk analysis.

questions.stem: What distinguishes an issue from a risk?

options.a: An issue has already occurred, whereas a risk may or may not occur.
options.b: An issue affects cost, whereas a risk affects time.
options.c: An issue is owned by the sponsor, whereas a risk is owned by the team.
options.d: An issue must be recorded, whereas a risk need not be.

questions.explanation: Certainty is the discriminator. Everything else — recording, ownership, which constraint is hit — applies to both.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stage in a typical issue resolution process?

options.a: Assessing the probability of the issue occurring.
options.b: Re-baselining the schedule to absorb the issue.
options.c: Auditing the configuration library for accuracy.
options.d: Escalating the issue to the appropriate level of authority.

questions.explanation: Identify, assess impact, escalate, resolve, close. The 'assess the probability' distractor is impossible by definition — an issue has already occurred, so it has no probability.

questions.stem: Which of the following defines quality?

options.a: The level of satisfaction stakeholders express with the project team.
options.b: The fitness for purpose of outputs, and the degree to which they meet requirements.
options.c: The value for money that the project achieves for its sponsor.
options.d: The complete absence of defects in a delivered product.

questions.explanation: Fitness for purpose, judged against agreed requirements — not perfection, and not price. Quality is relative to what was specified.

questions.stem: The purpose of quality management is to ensure that:

options.a: the project's outputs and the processes used to produce them meet the required standards.
options.b: deliverables are produced at the lowest achievable cost.
options.c: the project completes ahead of its baselined schedule.
options.d: every stakeholder personally approves each deliverable.

questions.explanation: Note that quality management covers both the outputs and the processes — that dual scope is what separates it from quality control alone.

questions.stem: Quality planning involves:

options.a: auditing the project's processes for compliance with organisational standards.
options.b: recording and tracking defects identified during testing.
options.c: inspecting completed deliverables against their specification.
options.d: determining the standards, acceptance criteria and processes that the project will apply.

questions.explanation: Planning sets the standard up front. The inspection distractor is quality control and the process-audit one is quality assurance — all three appear as each other's distractors throughout LO8.

questions.stem: Quality control is concerned with:

options.a: inspecting, measuring and testing outputs against their acceptance criteria.
options.b: providing confidence that the correct processes are being followed.
options.c: deciding whether the business case remains viable at a decision gate.
options.d: setting the quality standards that the project will work to.

questions.explanation: Control is done to the product, after the fact. Assurance is done to the process, during. Three words to hold apart: plan the standard, assure the process, control the product.

questions.stem: The purpose of quality assurance is to provide confidence that:

options.a: every individual deliverable has been separately tested.
options.b: the project will be delivered within its approved budget.
options.c: no defects will occur at any point during delivery.
options.d: the processes being used will produce outputs that meet the requirements.

questions.explanation: Assurance is confidence in the process, and it is usually provided by someone independent of the delivery team.

questions.stem: The purpose of a post-project review is to:

options.a: decide whether the project should be authorised to proceed to its next phase.
options.b: capture lessons learned and assess how well the project was managed.
options.c: verify that the project complied with the organisation's quality standards.
options.d: confirm that the expected business benefits have actually been realised.

questions.explanation: Every option here is an item named in outcome 8.6: authorising the next phase is a decision gate, confirming benefits is a benefits review, and verifying compliance is a project audit. This outcome asks you to hold four purposes apart — expect one of them, and know which is which.

questions.stem: Communication can be defined as:

options.a: the exchange of information between parties, and confirmation that understanding is shared.
options.b: the distribution of progress reports to stakeholders on a fixed schedule.
options.c: the recording of decisions taken during project meetings.
options.d: the process of persuading stakeholders to support the project.

questions.explanation: The confirmation half is the part candidates drop. Information sent is not communication until it has been received and understood.

questions.stem: One advantage of face-to-face communication is that it:

options.a: allows non-verbal signals to be observed and responded to.
options.b: removes the need for a communication plan.
options.c: always produces a written record of what was agreed.
options.d: is the least expensive option for a geographically dispersed team.

questions.explanation: Body language, tone and immediate feedback are the face-to-face advantages. The 'written record' distractor is an advantage of physical (written) communication — the three methods each have their own list.

questions.stem: One disadvantage of virtual communication is that it:

options.a: never leaves any record of what was discussed.
options.b: cannot be used with stakeholders outside the organisation.
options.c: depends on technology being available and reliable for everyone involved.
options.d: requires all participants to be in the same physical location.

questions.explanation: Technology dependency, plus weaker non-verbal cues, are the virtual disadvantages. The other three options are simply untrue, which is typical of the weaker distractors in LO9.

questions.stem: Which of the following would typically be included in a communication plan?

options.a: The delegated tolerances that trigger issue escalation.
options.b: The critical path through the project schedule.
options.c: Who receives which information, when they receive it, and by what method.
options.d: The acceptance criteria for each project deliverable.

questions.explanation: Audience, content, frequency, method, and who is responsible for sending it. If an option describes an artefact from another process, it is not communication plan content.

questions.stem: One benefit of a communication plan to a project manager is that it:

options.a: removes the need to carry out stakeholder analysis.
options.b: transfers responsibility for project reporting to the PMO.
options.c: guarantees that all stakeholders will agree with the project's decisions.
options.d: ensures the right stakeholders receive relevant information at the right time.

questions.explanation: A plan makes communication deliberate rather than reactive. It cannot manufacture agreement — watch for 'guarantees' and 'all'.

questions.stem: Leadership can be defined as the ability to:

options.a: hold formal authority over the members of a project team.
options.b: allocate tasks to team members and monitor their completion against the plan.
options.c: establish vision and direction, and to influence and align others towards a common purpose.
options.d: resolve disputes that arise between the project team and its suppliers.

questions.explanation: Vision, direction, influence, alignment. Note that leadership is explicitly not the same as formal authority — the 'holds formal authority' distractor is the trap for anyone equating the two.

questions.stem: Which action by a project team leader is most likely to improve the performance of the team?

options.a: Avoiding open discussion of conflict within the team.
options.b: Setting clear roles, responsibilities and objectives for each member.
options.c: Restricting information to only those members who must act on it.
options.d: Allocating work according to availability rather than skill.

questions.explanation: Clarity of role, openness and trust are the levers named in the syllabus. The three distractors are all recognisable anti-patterns — this outcome tends to be tested by making the wrong answers plainly wrong.

questions.stem: Which of the following are challenges for a project manager developing and leading a project team?
items: Team members reporting to more than one manager
Members joining and leaving as the project progresses
Team members being co-located for the whole project
Differences in skills, experience and working styles

options.a: 2, 3 and 4
options.b: 1, 2 and 4
options.c: 1, 2 and 3
options.d: 1, 3 and 4

questions.explanation: Co-location is a help, not a challenge — it is the dispersed team that creates difficulty. Spot the single positive item in the list and eliminate every option containing it.

questions.stem: In Tuckman's model of team development, which stage is characterised by conflict as members challenge roles and ways of working?

options.a: Performing.
options.b: Storming.
options.c: Norming.
options.d: Forming.

questions.explanation: Forming (polite and tentative), storming (conflict), norming (settled roles), performing (effective delivery). Match the stage to the described behaviour, not to the position in the sequence.

questions.stem: A project manager needs a team member who will generate original ideas and solve difficult problems creatively. Which of Belbin's team roles is the best fit?

options.a: Completer finisher.
options.b: Resource investigator.
options.c: Plant.
options.d: Implementer.

questions.explanation: The plant is the creative idea generator. Implementer turns ideas into action, completer finisher polishes and checks, resource investigator looks outside the team for contacts and opportunities.
